I would particularly like to thank Glen Harmer, who is the president of the Thunder Bay branch as well as the national president. I also want to thank a member of the Thunder Bay police force who was there at my request and with the permission of the chief. Bill S-8 deals with a number of relatively minor but important elements in the Motor Vehicle Safety Act. They are gaps that have been in the system that the government is wisely moving to correct.
There are new child restraint safety regulations so they can control that add-on. They can ensure that if there is a recall there is consumer registration, et cetera. Another positive move is the government's ability to control the standards for all-terrain recreation vehicles.
Too often we find that a vehicle that was bought for the bush is used on the roads. It may be in unsafe condition and whether it was used illegally or not it is appropriate that we control the manner of the manufacturing. The increase in fines for corporations from $200,000 to $1 million and for individuals from $5,000 to $10,000 is also quite appropriate. It brings it in line with some of the other acts we have passed in this House.
February 18, 1993

We may want to look in committee at putting some kind of COLA clause in there; a CPI link so we do not have to amend that part some time in the future.
There is the whole question of emission credits and averaging. I am not going to go into any detail but we have looked at that. We think it makes sense within the automotive industry. We do not believe it is necessarily the answer for smoke-stack industries. Within the automotive sector it will allow for implementation of clean air controls without harming the economic viability of the companies or forcing them to scrap equipment that is already on line but due to be phased out within a year or two.
There is also the ability to follow up if there is an imperfection in the manufacture of a pollution control element of an automobile. You can do a recall on that. Currently, as I understand it, the act does not provide for that opportunity.
There are a couple of areas I want to focus on that have been raised with me, not just in the context of this bill but in the context of the need to ensure that whatever is on the road is safe.
I want to start with what I will refer to as wrecks. These are cars that have been totalled and normally end up in the junk yard. We have a lot of folks in this country and I suspect in the United States who take those cars, cannibalize them, recycle them if you like, and in a lot of cases those recycled cars are not as safe as the new cars. I am advised if you weld the frame on a vehicle and it is not done right, in an impact you are actually jeopardizing the lives of the occupants or the occupants of the vehicle with which you have collided.
Under the Constitution at the manufacturing end it is the federal government's responsibility. Once the car or truck is built anything beyond that is the responsibility of the provinces. We need to find a way to impose a national standard on the provinces. One of the ways suggested in this bill is the use of a national safety mark. Whether it is a tire or a vehicle built according to Canadian federal standards developed under this act, they will get a safety mark that says this is a safe vehicle. It will be similar to the CSA putting a tag on our appliances because they have passed with approval.
I want to explore this concept in committee. If a vehicle has the national safety mark and is wrecked, we have to be able to remove that mark and develop a system so that before that vehicle can be put back on the road it must go through some kind of process to make
Government Orders
sure it is a functioning automobile that is structurally sound.
The province of Quebec, I understand, has a system whereby if a vehicle is wrecked and someone wants to put it back on the road when they go into the licence issuer they have to bring a photograph of that vehicle on what is called a full-body frame. Instead of somebody repairing the vehicle in the back yard it proves they have gone to an authorized repair facility which uses the most up-to-date equipment and has the knowledge of the integrity of the structure. They can therefore assure the licence issuer that this vehicle complies with, in that case, Quebec standards. I would like to see us do that on a national basis.
We have all seen these folks in our communities, at least in the rural and northern communities, who decide it is really neat to put tires on a car or truck that are five or ten times the size of what is supplied at the manufacturing level. In other words, the vehicle has been redesigned by the owner and does not meet the safety requirements or certainly the manufacturer's requirements. I think we can use the national safety mark as a mechanism to prevent that from occurring. The moment they add those monster truck tires, they would lose that safety mark and the car or truck would not be certified by the provinces.
Under this act we are also managing the trade of used automobiles between Canada and the United States. Under the free trade agreement, American-produced used cars are able to come into Canada. Until the free trade agreement very few cars came across. This bill sets out the requirements for those vehicles. They must meet Canadian standards. It is a way of managing this particular trade deal until the FTA is abrogated, but that is for another debate at another time.
It is designed to ensure that any vehicle imported meets Canadian standards, U.S. safety recalls apply and there is a consistency of labelling.
I would like to suggest there is a gap in this particular aspect as well. If I went to Duluth, Minnesota, bought a used car and brought it to the Canadian border I would only have to sign a declaration at the border that I was going to get any deficiencies fixed. There is no provision to ensure that those changes are done by the appropriate personnel. I could do them in my own back yard, or I could just say I had done them. I think we need an amendment to ensure that anyone bringing a vehicle across the border has to take it to a body shop, if it is something like a bumper replacement or a service station.

February 18, 1993
Government Orders
In Ontario there are various types of licences issued to certified mechanics licensed by the province of Ontario, and I am sure it is the same in other provinces. Let us make sure the vehicle goes through some kind of third party who can attest to the fact that the work has been done and the vehicle is safe to drive in Canada.
The final point I want to make concerns the question of wrecks coming here from the United States. Under this act wrecks will be allowed in. I argued that any Canadian wrecks should go through some kind of certification process and I believe American wrecks should be forced to undergo the same process as well. That may be another way we can set a national standard that is easily adhered to or adopted by the provinces.
Those are the areas I will raise in committee. There may be one or two witnesses we wish to call. I think this bill is an important one and it is not my intention to drag out the committee review, but I think we need to take a specific look at some of these elements so we can improve the bill.
Hun. Chas. L. Caccia (Davenport): Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House we would like to congratulate the senators for initiating this measure. It is a bill that will obviously help clear the air in our Canadian cities and rural Canada. It is a measure that is badly overdue which has been promised since 1989.
In our presentation today we would first like to examine what is generally understood about car emissions and put that into a particular framework.
Generally speaking, there is an impression that so long as car emissions are diluted they are not damaging to human health. Therefore idling a car, for instance, or accelerating, excessive burning of fuel in other words, is something that one should not pay too much attention to because it will dissolve and go up into the air.
This notion has to be dealt with because the emissions from a car contain a number of extremely dangerous substances. Therefore, the motor vehicle is a very convenient means of transportation that burns substances that are profoundly poisonous and dangerous to human health and to certain types of crops and agricultural activities, which I will mention later.
In examining the environmental damage, one finds out that the combustion of fossil fuels has an impact on the question of climate change, particularly because of the production of ozone. There is also the production of heavy metals and the pollution that is attributable to the toxic substances contained in gasoline and other transport fuels.
It is a well-known fact that the burning of gasoline and petroleum products through motor vehicle engines does contribute to the creation of smog, particularly from cars. The formation of smog in the urban setting and also in densely populated areas outside the urban setting can lead and has led to damaged crops and to poor quality air in our urban centres; so much so that sometimes in the summer there are excessive measurements of pollution in the cities, which in good part is attributed to ozone and other forms of pollution emanating from motor vehicle activity.
The substances in question are carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, ozone, toxic chemicals, lead, benzene, formaldehyde and polyaromatic hydrocarbons. In essence, carbon monoxide interferes with the blood's ability to absorb oxygen and it impairs the perception and thinking ability of humans. It has the capacity to slow reflexes. It can cause drowsiness, and in high concentrations it can even lead to death.
Nitrogen dioxide can increase the susceptibility to viral infections such as influenza, irritate the lungs, and cause bronchitis and pneumonia.
Ozone is one of the pollutants formed by the burning of gasoline and related substances. Ground level ozone irritates the respiratory system, causing coughing, choking, impaired lung functioning, reduced resistance to colds and possibly pneumonia. In some cases, the medical profession has identified chronic heart disease, asthma, bronchitis and even emphysema as being attributable to the burning of gasoline and related substances.
February 18, 1993

In the case of toxic emissions and metals one must underline the importance of the presence of lead in gasoline. In Canada we have reduced the amount of lead in gasoline in recent years. We could still further reduce it to the standards the Americans have reached and thus improve the quality of air and the health conditions of our population, particularly of children. Other chemicals that are found in gasoline are cadmium and asbestos, which collect on the roads through the wear and tear of tires, through the activity of brakes and the use of clutches and the wearing of clutch linings.
That can cause nerve damage in children and even in expectant mothers. Cadmium is suspected to cause cancer. With regard to asbestos, although the question is hotly debated, it may cause lung cancer.
This background is simply intended to put on record and demonstrate the fact that we are dealing with activities dangerous to human health and the environment. We can now briefly analyse the substance of the bill.
The requirements in the bill for the reduction of emissions would allow us to achieve new standards which will reduce emissions by up to 60 per cent per kilometre driven. That is a welcome measure. Under the scheme envisaged in the bill new cars would produce .25 grams of nitrogen oxide per each kilometre compared to the present .62. That is reduction by over half.
The production of hydrocarbons will be reduced from .25 grams to .16. Carbon monoxide levels will remain unchanged.
The point of contention does not so much concern reduction, although it could be improved, as the timetable. The question is when this measure will come into effect, which the minister unfortunately did not answer in the course of his introductory speech.
In 1989 the then Minister of the Environment and Minister of Transport promised to have these standards incorporated in this particular bill by 1994. We find out today that these measures will instead come into effect by 1996, and this is a very disturbing factor. In other words, the government made a commitment with a target date of 1994 but now finds itself in the position of postponing the date of enforcement until 1996 because of the slowness in producing this legislation. That is
Government Orders
highly regrettable, because it is at the expense of public health.
Another aspect of this bill that is a cause of concern is that the government, having promised binding regulations, has now produced a voluntary agreement by way of a memorandum of understanding with industry. This memorandum of understanding is not legally enforceable. We therefore find ourselves in a situation in which what is being proposed through the legislation and subsequently through the regulations may be implemented but may not be. It will depend on the good will of the parties concerned.
That approach leaves much to be desired. A piece of legislation should instead be passed by the Parliament of Canada in the interest of public health which is written in a manner that gives an assurance to the public that what is contained in the bill will rather than may take place. The difference between the two can be considerable.
The third point that must be raised here today is the question of permitting the industry to average emissions. In other words, certain fleets and certain models of cars would be above permitted standards and certain others would be below and the average between the two, so long as it meets the over-all standards, would then be accepted. In other words, certain types of cars would be polluting more and certain types of cars would be polluting less.
This type of approach is not very clever and is not very good for human health or the environment. This point was stressed in a submission presented by the AirWatch program of the Canadian Acid Precipitation Foundation from Toronto. When it appeared before the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee in June of last year it drew this particular question to the attention of concerned parties.
I would like to put on the record a paragraph from its brief that enunciates the position with which I concur:
This bill amounts to legislative sleight of hand, which would allow
the department and the industry to increase emissions by employing
emissions averaging methods already rejected in the United States.
The averaging approach is the issue on which this non-governmental group focused in particular. It specifies the problem in the following manner:

February 18, 1993
Government Orders
Under a vehicle-by-vehicle standard, individual vehicles must each meet a certain emission standard. To do this, there must be a margin between the actual amount of pollution produced by each vehicle, and the standard, in order to ensure compliance and to avoid recalls. Under an averaging system, the same margin must exist for some vehicles, but other vehicles can be allowed to exceed the standards. Depending on where such non-complying vehicles are sold, how many are produced, and the amount by which they exceed the supposed standard, additional pollution can be produced, and air quality problems can be aggravated.
The point to be made, and it is an important one, is that instead of emissions averaging, as this bill proposes, we would urge the government to have standards that would be applied to each car, vehicle by vehicle. Then public health and environmental concerns would be met in a far superior and more satisfactory manner.
Another point that needs to be made in connection with this bill is the moot question as to the importation of used cars in the proposed NAFTA area. Suppose that used cars will be imported from Mexico and the United States. These cars would already be of a certain age. Whose standards would these imported cars be expected to meet? They will probably be quite cheap. They will be quite appealing. However, they could be highly polluting vehicles and their presence in the marketplace could constitute a considerable threat to air quality and human health.
The issue here is one of balancing a variety of interests. The government with respect to the economic aspect of this issue, another key point, has come down in favour of allowing in clause 8 of the bill payment in exchange for permission to increase tailpipe emissions.
In other words, what the government is proposing is the introduction of the polluter pays principle. That in itself would not be a bad thing if we were to know what the polluter will pay and how the funds collected by way of this principle will be used. Will they be earmarked for additional pollution reduction, pollution research and other initiatives that will help reduce pollution in that industry?
I would argue, and it is a point that needs to be made in this debate, that the polluter pays principle is all right if the fee to be charged will discourage the polluter. If the fee to be charged will be such that the polluter will pay his way into polluting in having paid that fee, that fee will not act as a disincentive. That principle will not be
served and will not be implemented in the manner that it was originally intended by those who introduced it some time ago.
It should be clear that by charging a fee that is too low, you would just provide a licence to the polluter to continue to pollute. Under this bill, instead of charging a fee that is a disincentive to pollute, you would be applying the polluter pays principle in its original intent and meaning.
Therefore, it is incumbent upon us in the opposition to make this point in the hope that when the bill is examined in committee at second reading it will be given a thorough analysis. The section dealing with the matter of fees to be charged for vehicle emissions permits will be examined appropriately. The fees that will be charged for permission to produce excess pollution should be such that instead of becoming licences to pollute, they will become disincentives to pollute.
I am sure that there are members in this Chamber in all parties who would agree with this point. They would see the distinction between the two approaches.
To summarize our presentation, I will put it in those terms. We have a history of lagging behind the United States with respect to progressively implementing motor vehicle emission standards. This step is highly desirable and overdue. Second, we regret very much that the full deadline for implementation has been moved from 1994, as promised, to 1996.
The emission averaging as proposed in this bill, my third point, would result in increased vehicle emissions rather than in reductions. The alternative to this would be an enforcement of a vehicle by vehicle standard approach.
This legislation creates the authority for a vehicle manufacturer to pay fees in exchange for permission to possibly produce excess pollution. If that is going to be the net effect of this legislation, then this legislation regrettably will have failed its own purpose as set out in the preamble.
Having put these points in as concise a manner as possible and seeing that you would like to hear another voice on stage, thank you for your patience and your attention.
February 18, 1993

Mr. Speaker, in beginning my remarks on this speech, I would like to express my appreciation for the process that brings a very progressive bill like this one to us from the Senate to the House of Commons. I would like to pay tribute to the work of Senator Murray and Senator Oliver in the Senate who carried this bill through the committee and through the Senate and delivered it on June 19, 1992, for my birthday.
I hope for my next birthday on June 19 we will be able to have the regulations complete and the act in place, all in a good cause of cleaner air for Canadians.
This is an area in which I have considerable interest, quality of life issues, not just for the Fraser Valley where I live and where it is very important, but around the globe as a major issue that is carried forward by global parliamentarians on human settlements and particularly our emphasis toward developing sustainable cities programs.
The updating of this act is very significant because it reflects contemporary concerns regarding climate change and sustainable development. Therefore it is appropriate and not just for Canada. It is an initiative in co-operation with global discussions that came out of Rio and so forth.
This is of particular interest in the major cities of Canada, Toronto, Montreal, and above all Vancouver because greater Vancouver is located in the Georgia Puget Basin which is very akin to Los Angeles. Each of them is in a valley reservoir of rapid growth, confined geographically by mountains that produce air inversions. Along with ever increasing car emissions, over one million cars cross the bridges of Vancouver each day.
As we put these combinations of factors together, we do not want the Fraser Valley to become Los Angeles north. In fact that has to be a major fight, a major voice and a major reason why I stand here in the House of Commons.
The very basic essence of life is the quality of our air and the quality of our water. The quality of the airshed of the bioregion of Georgia Puget Basin, now with 4.5 million people, is intensely threatened daily as that population over the next 20 years doubles from 4.5 million to over 10 million people.
Government Orders
We do have in the greater Vancouver region a particular interest and concern that this bill be introduced, passed and more important, made effective. The nitrogen oxides, which are a key factor in causing ground level ozones, are released into our environment during the combustion of fossil fuels including gasoline, diesel, natural gas and coal. Nationally both nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, which are the major contributing agent of ozone, are both projected to grow by about 6 per cent between 1985 and the year 2005. If no new controls are developed to combat this problem, more problem areas will merge throughout our country and our globe.
California needs credit here because California has realized this difficulty and has legislation in place to deal with the problem, including laws mandating the sale of minimum percentages of zero emission vehicles and the maintenance of supply of alternative fuels to power these vehicles at gasoline stations.
California also has credible marketable credits for exceeding emission requirements. These credits allow for the attainment of the over-all policy objective at a lower cost to society because of efficient gains reaped by market allocation of these credits. I am pleased to see that this legislation follows that basic idea.
Canada must follow this lead before it becomes too late to save our air quality, particularly in our cities. Our approach must, however, be somewhat different in order to deal with the jurisdictional realities and constitutional differences between our countries.
We must have not only action at our national level in this form but joint action with the provinces that would permit the problem to be addressed in a more comprehensive fashion and that is the effective approach that we should take.
Our cities will only be made sustainable if we can combine the constitutional and jurisdictional responsibilities of the national government, the provinces and of our local governments, including our regional districts.
We must change this format, but until we can change it, we must operate respecting those jurisdictions, as I believe this bill has done.
An approach I strongly believe that Canada should take to deal with this problem would be by encouraging the development and sale of either ethanol of electrical

February 18, 1993
Government Orders
powered vehicles. I am pleased that the research in this area is moving quite dramatically.
In fact, if you take the issue of electric vehicles, all the major car companies of the world are producing prototypes in this area. This prototype research is important and needs to be encouraged through incentives and of course through regulation and legislation.
When you think in terms of not just the research where in low emission vehicles, zero emission vehicles and electric vehicles there is encouraging results that are gained through vehicles like the Los Angeles car which is a combination of gas and electric, or some of the newer technologies that are looking at alternate fuels. Mazda, for example, is showing in Ottawa and Eastern Canada Day at the car shows. It is showing a rotary engine combined with a metal hydride fuel tank. This Mazda car uses hydrogen gas.
Nissan and others are working with liquid hydrogen fuel and the many other kinds of possibilities. All of these present particular problems. The particular problems they create are the problems of supply of fuel, whether that supply is found at the electrical level at residences or the need to have fuel supplied for whichever of the alternate fuels are required for the new vehicles, the new prototypes.
The method of approach in this bill I think is particularly useful. Bill S-8 proposes the use of emission credits as a tool for implementing tighter emission standards. Emission credits have been very effective incentives for encouraging manufacturers in California to produce zero emission vehicles.
The possibility of selling credits also encourages the development of desirable zero emission vehicles by permitting the recovery of some development costs from competitors.
I think the point that was made by the member for Davenport is a valid and interesting point that needs to be explored further and that is the question of how do you apply them? Do you apply them through averaging of vehicles or do you apply them on the basis of specific individual vehicles? This would vary from province to province according to the capacity of a province to have motor vehicle testing stations, if you are dealing on a vehicle by vehicle basis. Perhaps there could be an application in co-operation with the provinces. To start
with the concept of averaging is appropriate and probably all we can achieve at this stage. However, I think we should look in the direction of ultimately testing individual vehicles as well.
This is an area of opportunity, an opportunity to consider the North American free trade agreement. President Clinton will sign the North American free trade agreement, but he has suggested parallel agreements on the environment. Vice-President Gore has been particularly strong in this area. It is an area where we can demonstrate leadership through this bill. In fact, the bill does have the flexibility to adapt to certification and international standards of other countries. This is a place where we could find agreement.
As the parallel agreement on the environment is established with the free trade agreement, we need to rationalize the various laws and regulations of all three countries; Mexico, Canada and the United States. There could be a tendency toward two things in this parallel agreement: to take the lowest common denominator of all of the standards of each of the countries; or to take the highest common denominator. In other words, we would take the strongest regulations from Canada, the strongest regulations from the United States and the strongest regulations from Mexico, and put those as the standards for the North American continent.
I hope we will choose the high road and the highest possible standards for the regulations for all three countries. I hope those will be established in a parallel agreement to be signed along with the free trade agreement. I urge that we proceed in that direction.
I hope also that in the free trade agreement those parallel agreements will mean that competition among the countries will be on a level playing field because, in fact, we are all playing to the same standards.
A second element of the free trade agreement parallel accord that should be developed in air and vehicle emission standards should relate to enforcement. We can write this law but if we do not have the capacity to enforce it through the testing of vehicles and through the co-operation with manufacturers, then we have nothing. It is like a constitution; it means nothing if it is not enforced and applied.
*
February 18, 1993

Therefore, the regulations that go with this act are extremely significant. I would hope that the regulations can be looked at in committee because if you pass the act and the regulations are not stringent, then you have accomplished nothing or very little other than a statement of principle and intent. If I had my preference, I would put in this bill that the regulations be known at the same time as the bill is passed. In fact the government is working on regulations on the basis of the bill that it has produced. Therefore, I would like to see consideration given to putting some of those main regulations in the bill.
I recognize that we do not want the regulations to be so inflexible that we cannot change the standards as technology allows us to change them, but I think it is something we will need to consider in committee.
This bill is not the end, it is but a beginning, the first stage. In addition to that is the implementation process of this bill, taking us from prototypes in each of the experimental automobiles to the fleet situation, a situation where you try it in a large group of cars and then finally the broad public market. Government can help in this area.
I will be proposing two private member's bills in companion to this bill which suggest, for example, when the Government of Canada and our Crown corporations buy new automobiles, a percentage of these automobiles should be low emission vehicles or zero emission vehicles. If we are spending billions of dollars and of those billions of dollars a good portion are automobiles, why should the government not set the standard by buying these and use the fleet system that is necessary to carry us to the next stage?
For example, when you buy a hydrogen gas car, you have to find a gas station that sells hydrogen. You cannot expect every station suddenly to have hydrogen. If you use it through the fleet process, Crown corporations and governments will establish a central depot that these vehicles operate from and then that can be the middle stage. The co-operation of governments is required and I will bring in a private member's bill in to that effect.
Second, the bill has a sanction of tax on vehicles that in fact will raise some money hopefully. The tax is a disincentive. I think we should also have incentives. While the government might feel this is a bit of heresy it is my view that as an incentive to introduce electric
Government Orders
vehicles or alternate fueled vehicles we might allow an exemption from the GST.
If that kind of exemption could be given, it is a very high-profile exemption that says to people it is important to the quality of air that they should go out and buy one of these cars. To do that the Government of Canada will give the incentive right to the individual in the marketplace.
Second, we need a fast write-off for businesses. A business person should be able to get a write-off in one, two, or three years as opposed to five or ten years. Perhaps we would have a further incentive for business to go beyond the government corporations, the Crown corporations, to the business corporations and then to the individual in the market. I think we would have a considerable speed-up of moving from prototypes to reality and to a higher quality of air.
These are some ideas I have. This is pioneering the new world. This is pioneering the next century as we move to live in cities. Many of us are country boys with country values. We want clean air, clean water, a little green space in our cities. We want an efficient transportation system.
Would that I could will away my desire for a car but I am a North American male-and this would apply to the North American female-and when a North American male or female turns 16 the first thing they want, your children, my children, and me, conditioned or whatever it is, a car because a car is synonymous with freedom. You can try to defeat that and say to your son or daughter at age 16 "take a bus". Well you can try. You can try to say to yourself "take a bus" or get on the rapid transit. I think we need lots of support for rapid transit, but at the same time there is the reality of our passion for our cars. It is North American. It is Canadian. It is world wide. Look at China today, it is going from the bicycle to' the motorcycle, to what is highly desirable after the television set and the refrigerator is the car. This is true everywhere in the developing world.
You can fight that value and try to condition that value by saying get on your bicycle, get on the rapid transit but it will only sell in part. Therefore we must deal with the issue of cars themselves and that means electric cars. It means hydrogen gas cars, hydrogen liquefied fuel cars. Look at Mohawk and the great ethanol movement. It deserves a word of credit. You can drive by a Mohawk

February 18, 1993
Government Orders
station in Vancouver and put ethanol in your car. These are the very positive kinds of initiatives that governments need to reward. We are never going to take the car off of our roads in our time because it is a special symbol of freedom for young people, of prosperity, affluence and so forth. Therefore, we are going to have to deal with these alternatives.
On that basis, this is a futuristic bill. It deserves the support of all of us. It deserves that we should all look forward to this bill, not in the context of safety as it used to be drafted-that is part of the bill-but in the context of can we continue to live in the 21 megacities of the world whose quality air is depreciating and the major factor in that depreciation is auto emissions.
Members of the House and of the Senate, this is a great bill to proceed with. We must make the regulations stringent. I look forward to a cleaner, better world because we met and had this debate today.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Nicole Roy-Arcelin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity today to lead off the debate on third reading of Bill C-88, tabled in the House on June 18 last year, whose purpose is to amend the Copyright Act.
The bill reflects the main objective of the Copyright Act, which is to protect creative activity. When we say copyright, we no longer refer exclusively to printed works. Today, creative works are transmitted in a multitude of ways, as a result of the incredible technologies that have been developed in the past 20 years.
By amending the Copyright Act, we are trying to adapt the legislation to the present context. There have been radical changes in recent years, while the wording of the legislation remained practically unchanged from 1921 to 1988.
Bill C-88 proposes to amend a number of definitions contained in the Copyright Act. More specifically, it proposes to replace the obsolete definition of the term musical work, redefine performance and clarify the definition of the term network in order to determine who pays what to whom. For instance, the present legal definition of a musical work is "any combination of melody and harmony, or either of them, printed, reduced to writing or otherwise graphically produced or reproduced".
February 18, 1993

In fact, only music scores meet the current criteria for musical work. According to the amendment we are proposing, any form of musical composition, with or without words, will constitute a musical work in the meaning of the Copyright Act.
The Society of Composers, Authors and Musical Publishers of Canada, also known as SOCAN, collects royalties on behalf of authors and composers, both for the transmission of musical works to the public by means of telecommunications and for the public performance of such works.
The impact of technological change, which has also changed the way musical works are used, has been greatest on composers, authors and music publishers. Previously, the definition of a musical work or, should I say, a music score prevented SOCAN from collecting royalties for the transmission of musical works by specialized services and "paying" services.
This kind of transmission is meant when we refer to the right to communicate to the public by telecommunications. Bill C-88 makes a clear distinction between the right to communicate a musical work to the public by telecommunications and the right to do a public performance of the work, a distinction that is not made in the Copyright Act in its present form.
In making that distinction, the bill determines that payment must be made in return for exercising each of these rights. Bill C-88 ensures that everyone who transmits musical works and who takes an active part in their transmission, including programmers, cable companies, networks and their affiliated stations, is jointly and individually responsible for all payments chargeable for rights to communicate such works to the public by telecommunications.
This provision will simplify the equitable distribution of royalties to be collected pursuant to those rights. Failure to clarify the situation and ensure that the amendments proposed to the Copyright Act in 1989 are fully implemented will further increase the amount of royalties fore gone.
For artists, who are one of the least well-off groups in our society, the situation is a serious one. The government is determined to ensure that authors and composers of musical works are fairly remunerated for every use of their works, and I know members on both sides of the House support this objective.
Government Orders
By adopting Bill C-88 we will meet a commitment made to copyright holders. This measure will send a clear message that review and clarification of the Copyright Act, which has tremendous repercussions on the economic viability of this group, is a priority.
In concluding, on behalf of the Minister of Communications, I would like to thank all members of the legislative committee for their work on Bill C-88. As a result the process has been constructive and well timed. I would also like to thank all members of the House for their co-operation.

Mr. Speaker, it was a great pleasure for me to listen to the hon. member, who was a good witness for the interests of artists, especially those who appeared before us on the committee. I listened to you with pleasure. You spoke on behalf of the minister, because you are faithful to the committee and I am pleased to recognize that today.
[English)
The enhancement under Bill C-88, the act to amend the Copyright Act in this third reading comes finally after years and years of an absence of a right, which deprived artists particularly musical composers and writers from earning a fair livelihood through an error committed during the negotiations of the free trade agreement. Not only did the free trade agreement have negative fall-out in many other areas, certainly for the artistic community and those who write, produce and compose it has been a source of great irritation and an unnecessary degree of financial deprivation which I would think has concerned all of us.
Those people involved in this particular field, those song writers and composers, can really be very appreciative of the incessant pressure they have put on this government through their collective SOCAN. They were very articulate in explaining and expressing their deep and serious concerns. It has taken a long time and it took a strong friend of the government to really get this whole thing moving.
We are pleased to be standing here today and finding a mechanism to answer that concern and at the same time to acknowledge that the essence of copyright is the finding of a fair balance between the rights of the creators and the rights of the users.

February 18, 1993
Government Orders
I and the Liberal Party support this bill because in its present form it does represent what we consider to be the kind of fair balance between the rights of the song writers and composers and the people who make commercial use of music. Rights were denied and I think even though those rights were denied in error during the free trade implementation legislation procedure, it is nonetheless not too late. I hope to repair some of this very serious damage.
I must make an observation about copyright. My colleagues have heard me say only too often that it is the kind of legislation I hate to do. Most people do not understand what copyright is all about and its vital importance to the life of many people in terms of intellectual property. It is particularly important to Canadian artists, entertainers and creators in every field of their expression. It is also a subject of increasing importance to the welfare of our Canadian economy. The same holds true on the international scene today through the multilateral conventions.
I would like to draw to the attention of the minister some very important multilateral issues that are going to arise in Stockholm very shortly, I believe at the beginning of June. These will have serious implications for the audio-visual producers and for the song writers if we do not take a firm stand to protect their claims under the Berne convention, the Rome convention and to ensure that our American neighbours are supportive of the interests of the arts.
We already overlooked them once. We fought hard in order to protect our cultural industries through the free trade agreement. We got special concerns.
Today is a very important day in the life of the artists. They were here to express their very serious concerns about the underfunding and the cuts that have taken place in the field of artistic grants and contributions by this government over the last eight years.
They raised against the wall of the National Arts Centre that incredible banner of Canada on which
200,000	signatures had been affixed as the flag went across this land which indicates the importance expressed by Canadians who support the arts, buy tickets to the theatre, buy the records and the songs, who enjoy the plays. They recognize that our films, movies, videos and our television series are selling so well around the world
and that we have as a small country the most incredible talent everywhere.
Today is a very apt day to move once again into a field where there has not been adequate protection which in, of and by itself creates the low income our artists have to live with. In essence, it is the artists who are the best supporters of the arts of this country. It is the artists who not only produce but also have to sacrifice many things in life in order to allow their creative juices and talent to be expressed in a variety of ways.
To them we have to be very grateful for they mark our place on the global map as Canadians, as distinct, as unique. In a globalized world it is very important that we with the values we stand for express them through the screen, song and dance or in any variety of ways throughout the world. We should pay and respect these people to the best of our ability.
Today these artists and entertainers who are performing works across the country and around the world and in whom we take great pride bring into this country very important revenues. I do not know how many people realize the numbers of people involved in this field. Over
400,000	people work in this field.
We bring in over $17 billion in revenues to this country. We are about number four in the GDP of this country. About 2.6 per cent to 3 per cent of the GDP comes out of the field of art. It is the successes of artists like Roch Voisine, Bryan Adams and Celine Dion who are selling around the world. Their revenues come here and we take a good part of them in taxes and that helps the economy of this country. It is a business. Art is an expression. It is not a widget. It is a business, but it is a different form of business.
There are hundreds of names I could mention. These people are recognized by critics and audiences around the world. They are among the best in the world. When they sing, perform, write and compose, they do not get paid for their work if it appears on a cable system or on our network system. That is because of an error in law.
The artists have been losing millions and millions of dollars and I think that is grossly unfair. This is what the minister, this bill and this government were trying to shore up and fill in. It is its own error in the free trade agreement which it is trying to patch up now. I know we are pleased to participate in that.
February 18, 1993

Copyright protects their interests and enhances the cultural sovereignty of Canada. I do not think I need to go into a song and dance about that. If we did not have these cultural expressions, who and what would we be? Would we be extended Americans with no identity? It is happening fast enough. We need to really maintain this and who we are through the expression of these people. Copyright is important to business, as I said.
Intellectual property is the bedrock upon which we build our information-based society. It is critical to the future of this country. The accelerating pace of technological change demands greater ingenuity and creativity to compete in world markets. It is our knowledge that adds value to the goods and services we sell.
Canadians need a legislative framework to be able and capable of supporting these developments and defending the rights of Canadian creators.
Bill C-88 is another step toward the modernization of the Copyright Act. For some Canadian song writers and composers it is a very important step. It is by no means the major revision that is required in phase two of copyright that was promised before copyright phase one even came in. Although I am delighted that we have this revision, it is by far not the answer that we really need so that all forms of copyright are protected. Canadian artists and Canadian businesses can really be protected in the fullness of the intent.
The Canadian Independent Record Production Association in a recent newsletter called for phase two of this copyright reform. It reflects the current realities and enables creators to receive fair recompense for their work. I think this bill fills in a large part of the void that was highlighted.
I would like to read into the record what they had to say because I think it is important. They said: "It is extremely difficult to run an efficient, profitable business if the law allows users and consumers to use our property freely while negating the efforts and business acumen of our members. It seems unbelievable that such a gross injustice should continue to have been perpetrated over more than two decades, not just from the point of view of the lack of morality and disregard for the basic principles of justice and fairness that this implies, traits which are
Government Orders
supposed to be common to all Canadians, but equally important, the attitude toward intellectual property that ignores the inherent value to Canadian society of having a strong, value-added industry that will make a substantial contribution to Canada's future prosperity. We can but hope that 1993 will bring a long-awaited change in this unhappy situation and enable our sector to make the contribution to Canadian culture and export earnings it is capable of, given the proverbial level playing field of opportunity that it has long deserved".
Although this particular aspect of the bill will cover one small part, it certainly does not cover home taping, performing rights, neighbouring rights and many other rights which are yet to be discussed.
I asked today in the House during Question Period whether we were truly interested in the well-being of our arts, cultural institutions and artists. The bill we passed on June 8 last year gave artists the right to go before a tribunal and a tribunal was to have been set up so they could negotiate properly and in due form. The government has not seen fit to put that into place. It has not proclaimed that bill even though it has gone through the Senate and is law. It takes political will to name the judges for that tribunal. All that is left is political will.
Although we are debating and passing this bill today, I call on the government to realize it is one thing to put on a public face and lots of performance, but this box we are now presenting may be a Trojan Horse unless this bill is proclaimed into law and enacted upon. The tribunal for the artists has not been acted upon to date.
Cable companies that carry specialty services such as MuchMusic, MusiquePlus, YTV, Vision and Arts and Entertainment, that do not broadcast over the air, use the works of Canadian musicians without paying for them. Is that right? Would you like your works to be used without any recognition or pay? It does not put food on your table or pay your rent. This means that while song writers such as Gordon Lightfoot, Roch Voisine or whoever, might receive royalties for air play of a song on radio or on a broadcast television like CTV, TVA or CBC, there is no remuneration for their air play on channels such as MuchMusic, MusiquePlus, Nashville Network or other services which are available only on cable.

February 18, 1993
Government Orders
The whole reason for this is forgetfulness when the free trade agreement was negotiated, amongst other forgetfulnesses. I will not go into that. I can see you are smiling, Mr. Speaker. This is perhaps not the moment, but boy could I really enjoy a real debate on free trade.
Do it.

Do it, okay. How about you speaking for me over here?
This is an injustice as is any other service. Let us put this bill through and ensure that the errors that were about to be committed are not committed again by a minister ill-advised by his staff. This minister almost committed an error that would have caught nursing homes, hospitals, mom and pop shops and small businesses where they had a radio on or were playing a cassette because it would have been trapped under the gramophone act it had put in here.
I can say to you we got rid of the gramophone exemption. We then clarified the copyright issues around CTV. We hope we will not have to be concerned that there will be any kind of double payment and that we are severally and jointly considering responsibilities.
We will hopefully have the Canadian Copyright Board review the flat revenue tariff versus the incidental tariff that is presently in place as the payments system, in the interest of what is best for the artists involved.
I hope this copyright bill will be the forerunner of phase two of copyright which is desperately needed. I certainly support the move of this bill into law.

Mr. Speaker, the fact that this is a short debate and there is all-party agreement to this government bill tells an interesting story. It is a story that is worth putting on the public record.
When the Standing Committee on Culture and Communications was holding hearings earlier last year on the state of the cultural industries in Canada which resulted in our unanimous report on The Ties that Bind, we heard presentations from SOCAN which is the Society of Composers, Authors, and Musical Publishers of Canada. We heard how a technical oversight in the drafting of the copyright law is costing them millions of dollars every year.
As the government person and the spokesperson for the Liberal Party have also pointed out, the problem was
that the old copyright law defined a musical work as having a written score. The cable companies were saying; "we are not transmitting a written score. We are transmitting sound".
In the old copyright law, the definition of broadcasting was something that was broadcasted over the air. The cable companies were saying; "but we are not broadcasting over the air, we are broadcasting by wire".
They were using the works of song writers, composers and authors without paying one cent in royalties. I suppose the other television companies like CBC and CTV, Global and so forth could have also said: "Well, we are not transmitting something that is written". But they did not. They lived within the intent and spirit of the law, unlike the cable companies.
I initially suggested to my fellow members on the committee that we have a quick little amendment to plug this. It was obvious that all members from all political parties who were at that committee hearing were convinced this was an unacceptable situation. It was stupid. Why not have a quick little amendment to change this and rectify the situation?
We invited the government to bring in the bill that is in front of us, although it is not quite the bill in front of us. There was full co-operation of all political parties and members on our committee and we worked in a co-operative way together. It is an example on how Parliament can and should operate and what we accomplished demonstrates what a truly representative system can do.
Also interesting was the interference from the department and bureaucrats, although not from the minister. I would like to separate the minister from the bureaucrats, although I was not privy to all the communications. My criticisms were of the bureaucrats from the department. Instead of presenting us with a bill to plug those loopholes as we wanted, they brought us a bill that also had a whole bunch of other bells and whistles attached to it.
They wanted us to tackle the whole question of what is commonly called the gramophone exemption. This is an exemption in the existing law that would allow a restaurant or a public place to play a gramophone and not be charged royalties. It is outdated and has to be addressed but this was not the place.
February 18, 1993

Organizations like the Restaurant Association et cetera made a valid submission to our committee asking us to leave it as it is right now. We have to discuss this whole other area in phase two of copyright. Do not take this little part that has to be reformed and try to do it. Leave it because there are some interesting questions.
I used to operate a restaurant and would turn the radio on in the kitchen to listen to music. Now is that commercial exploitation? Should I be paying royalty for that? I do not believe so, but if I was running a fancy restaurant and tuned into an FM station that just played certain types of music, if it was important for me in terms of creating the ambience of my commercial establishment and I was making money off somebody else's creative work, then yes I should pay some royalty for that.
These are some very fundamental principles and we have to debate them. I urge the government to proceed with phase two of copyright. It is badly needed. I am critical of the government for delaying it so long but to deal with it in this particular piece of legislation is inappropriate.
Finally the department came with some further amendments. Those amendments in turn created a whole slew of other problems and then we started hearing from people who made films including educational films because the amendments the bureaucrats were introducing affected a whole group of other people. Finally we were able to convince the bureaucrats and the government to drop that section of the bill.
I thought everything was solved but then the last Wednesday before Christmas recess the committee was to deal with clause-by-clause considerations. Before we could proceed the government came up with a whole new set of amendments.
We began to wonder whether the government and the bureaucrats really wanted this. Every time they introduced these new amendments they created another road-block. This new amendment dealt with the definition of a network. I asked them if they had consulted and they said they had but when I went to the broadcasters they told me they had not been consulted.
Government Orders
You have to ask the question: Why did the government bureaucrats come in at the last moment with a whole new set of amendments that did not affect the intent and essence of the bill? My experience in copyright is that if you change even one part of it the ramifications can affect all sorts of different enterprises and groups you were not even aware of.
The only decent way of handling it is through a consultative process, an open process that holds hearings so all parties can appear before our committee and tell us the effects of whatever change is being proposed. We did not do it. The government came in at the last moment with a whole new set of amendments and did not allow us to listen to the broadcasters.
In this particular case, CTV would be directly affected. We have never heard from CTV how this amendment which is now in this bill is going to affect them. I think that is wrong and unfair. It is not the correct process. I am not certain if we really understand and know what this will mean until we hear from all interested parties.
I am very happy to see the bill and will not object to it, nor will I object to any parts of it. I suspect once I understood the implications and application of the amendment the government introduced at the very last moment, I would probably agree with it. I certainly did not want to be stampeded into it. I certainly did not want to make a decision on it without hearing all the affected parties. The government did not give us that opportunity-
Even though Bill C-88 is an example of where all political parties and parliamentarians from the government and the opposition can work together in harmony, it is also an example of how bureaucrats can interfere with that process. I want to put on record that there is a lesson to be learned from this.
I am happy we will be able to proceed with Bill C-88 and pass it in all stages, hopefully this afternoon. It corrects an injustice. It corrects a wrong. It establishes some fairness, some justice and some equity for important citizens of our society, the creators of musical works that we listen to, musical works that are like mirrors of ourselves and society.

February 18, 1993
Private Members' Business
It does not solve all the problems. It certainly does not solve all the severe problems of the artistic community in this recessionary time and in a period of increasing government cutbacks. The cutback to the Department of Communications by 10 per cent this year and 10 per cent next year across the board will have devastating implications and applications.
When granting agencies like the Canada Council have to scale back it means that some orchestras, some theatre groups and some galleries will not be able to continue, and that is unfortunate. It is not just unfortunate for the cultural life, the image of our country and our self-awareness as a country, but it has negative economic implications.
My colleague from the Liberal Party, the Liberal critic for culture, put on record some of the economic factors involved. Earlier today in my statement to the House I went into some of the economic factors. Almost 350,000 people are employed in the industry. Some say it is almost 400,000 people. It contributes some $17 billion to economic activity in Canada or some 2.5 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product. These are significant economic realities.
The arts, the culture, artists, musicians, writers and actors make a tremendously important contribution to the psyche of the country and to the economics of the country. We earn in Canada in terms of our foreign balance of payments from the arts some $1.7 billion from people offshore who bought our records, our movies, our books, et cetera. For us to cut back in this important economic activity is counterproductive.
These are the arguments. These are the debates. These are the battles I am sure will be fought in this House on other occasions and during the election campaign whenever that occurs. However today we are united. There is total unanimity of all members of the House in urging the passage of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, since there is only a minute left and we would like to pass this bill today, I would like to say that the Bloc Quebecois fully supports this bill and even congratulates all parties in the House for co-operating so much in order that
authors can earn a living from what they do. We are ready to vote.
