that Bill C-336, an act to amend the Criminal Code and the Young Offenders Act (absence of criminal liability of child under 10 years of age and definition of child and young person), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to present a private bill that I feel addresses a flaw in our justice system.
I would like to take a look at the purpose of the bill. It is specifically to reduce the age for the operation of the Young Offenders Act from the current 12 years of age to 10 years of age. That requires two specific statutory amendments.
The first is that section 13 of the Criminal Code will have to be amended to reduce the age of criminal responsibility from the current 12 to 10. Second, it will require a change in the Young Offenders Act of the definition of a young person from the current 12 to 17 year age group to 10 to 17 and describe as a child a person who is under 10 years of age.

February 18, 1993

A little background would be useful in understanding why I propose this amendment. The Young Offenders Act was enacted in 1984. Prior to that act, offences by young persons were covered by the Juvenile Delinquents Act which covered youths aged 7 to 18. In effect, after 1984 youths aged 7 to 11 simply dropped out of the justice system. It was believed at that time that child welfare legislation would be sufficient to regulate their affairs even if those affairs involved ciminality.
In any event, now the public knows that the Young Offenders Act has more than one problem. Many people have suggested that we should change the name. Let us be honest. Changing the name of the statute will not do anything. We have to address the real problems in the statute.
As I see it there are at least two flaws-there are others-in the current act. It is odd that just a year ago the House passed an amendment to the Young Offenders Act. We were told at that time by the government that the act would address the flaws in the Young Offenders Act. I say that is not true. It did not address them and it was only a superficial response. We still have work to do.
The criminal justice net currently excludes crimes by those who are under 12 years of age. Not only do we have the scope or net problem where acts by those individuals escape the system, but to many the act appears not to have any teeth. It is ineffective. That is not just a perception; that is a reality.
If one looks at the principles contained in the Young Offenders Act, and I will simply cheriy-pick through, one reads things like: The youth have special needs and require guidance and assistance; it is not inconsistent with the protection of society to take no measures or take measures other than judicial proceedings; young persons should have special guarantees of their rights and freedoms; rights and freedoms of young persons include a right to the least possible interference with freedom that is consistent with the protection of society. The act shall be liberally construed to mean that young persons will be dealt with in accordance with the principles, some of which I just enunciated. In the end we can see that in those principles there is no principle of general or specific deterrence to young offenders contained in the act, none at all. If there is no goal, if there is no deterrence, the act has no teeth for that age group.
Private Members' Business
Let us move now to the amendment I propose: the lowering of the age from 12 years to 10 years to include young offenders. Let us take a look at what has been happening with the under-12 group over the last few years.
In 19911 received a letter from a principal in my riding of Scarborough-Rouge River. I will just read a portion of it because it is very instructive. He wrote: "A 10-year old boy in my adjustment class assaulted seven girls" and he described the sexual offence, sexual assault. "While discussing the problem with him he went into a rage, physically assaulting, kicking, punching, biting my viceprincipal, social worker and myself. He threatened to return with a gun and shoot me. He was suspended. The following week he returned with a bb gun or pellet gun. I was out of the school at a meeting so he threatened several students with it and followed two of the above-mentioned girls home".
He described the action that the school took including a suspension and informing the Children's Aid Society. He continued: "My problem is the inability to deal with the incident as it affects society. The police inform us that they can do nothing because of the Young Offenders Act. They further stated that they probably could not even take away the gun. The Children's Aid Society has difficulty doing anything if the problem is not a threat to the boy himself. Threats to others are not their mandate".
In 1992 I had a letter from two teachers from another school. They said: "There have been increasing occurrences of theft in our classrooms. Children are stealing from other children as well as from adults. These children have no remorse about their actions. Some of these young children continue to commit these crimes on a regular basis and as a result we are dealing with property damage, home-made weapons, verbal abuse, physical abuse, harassment, intimidation. If we continue to excuse inappropriate behaviour from the above areas we will also continue to give students the message that their crimes are not serious enough and they will not be accountable for their actions. We feel that if students choose to commit crimes they should also be responsible for these actions and serve the proper punishment according to the law for all people".
That is just a sampling from my riding, but Scarborough is not alone. There is great frustration at the failure of the Young Offenders Act in every area of the country.

February 18, 1993
Private Members' Business
In August 1992 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, by a resolution at its annual conference, urged the Minister of Justice to review the application of the Young Offenders Act to include individuals under 12 years of age.
We have information from the Canadian Centre for Justice Statistics. It is a collection of data from 10 per cent of Canada's police forces. If we extrapolate-this is not scientific-from the data gathered by that centre for statistics we can estimate that there are approximately
14,000	otherwise criminal acts being committed by offenders under the age of 12. I call them offenders even though in law they are not offenders and even though in law those acts are not criminal offences.
I have some additional examples from that grouping. Last February The Ottawa Citizen reported the case of a five-year old girl who could not go to school because a ten-year old boy had slapped her and was threatening her with a knife. In September 1991 two serious incidents occurred, also in the Ottawa area. Four elementary school students, all under the age of 12, kidnapped, gagged and physically assaulted a seven-year-old. In the other incident a 10-year old boy was shot in the arm and leg by an 11-year-old.
In the 1989-90 year, the Ontario English Catholic Teachers Association conducted a survey of assaults upon teachers and students. Among other things, it found 664 incidents of common assault; 73 incidents of assault with a weapon, threatening with a weapon and serious physical injury and harassment; and 570 incidents of vandalism.
The number of those incidents are growing. I want to point out that many police will not either bother to report or act in relation to criminal acts committed by youths under 12 years of age because, they say: "It simply is not a crime. It is not a criminal offence. We do not have a criminal. We have not got a charge. We have not got a process. We cannot arrest. We cannot intervene. We cannot detain. The matter is closed". Many statistics just do not get reported.
In a report prepared in 1990 for the Department of Justice, it appears that there are recommendations from the governments of the provinces of Nova Scotia, Ontario and British Columbia, all recommending that the Young Offenders Act age be reduced to nine or ten years
of age. I point out that my bill would bring the age down to 10 years of age.
One of the problems cited in that study is the ineffectiveness of existing child welfare legislation in filling the gap in dealing with and responding to those kinds of offences by youths under 12 years of age. I do not have time to review the child welfare legislation in every province, but essentially child welfare legislation permits intervention by authorities only to protect the child. It is for the purpose of protecting the welfare of the child that the authorities can intervene, not for protection of the public.
When the intervention occurs generally, it must be by law in the following manner. They must take the child home to the parents or to a place of safety. That is only for the purpose of protecting the child. In many of the incidents I have mentioned there was not any question of any danger to the child involved. The child was a danger or had committed a criminal act in relation to someone else.
Therefore, in those instances where we think we can rely on child welfare legislation, there is no sanction, absolutely no sanction at all. What do we do when we take this offending child home to a family where there is no real family, when they do not care, when they do not know what to do? That child is simply given a free ride home with no sanction.
From the study prepared for the Department of Justice there were a number of reasons cited why the age should be reduced. Again, I will just cherry pick through some of those reasons. Some children under 12 are responsible for their actions and take advantage of their immunity from prosecution. They do have a criminal intent.
We could lower the age to prevent or to reduce the likelihood of older persons using under 12-year-olds to commit offences; to protect the public and to give consideration to victims; the need for consequences for the child when a law is contravened; the need for specific and general deterrents which are simply not in the system at all now, not even in the existing Young Offenders Act as it applies to all youth under the age of 18. There is not even any reference to general or specific deterrents in that act, let alone for the children who the act does not cover at all.
There is a need for more effective intervention, more effective than a simple referral to the child welfare system, and a need for some middle ground or alterna-
February 18, 1993

tive measures between returning a child home with no further action and referral to child welfare. The children will benefit from services available in the youth justice system as well as the controls possible with a court order like curfew, probation, non-association conditions.
There are many reasons why many observers think this act should be amended in the way I have proposed. I am not advocating that 10 and 11-year-olds be dealt with in adult court. No. I am simply asking that they go to youth court. I am not asking to send them to a maximum security institution but only that they be dealt with by the young offender system that is in place. It is the same place where we deal with 12, 13 and 14-year-olds.
I ask you to put yourself in the position of a parent of an 11-year-old who is either robbed, physically assaulted or sexually assaulted by a person of the same age with criminal intent. That person is simply met by someone and taken home.
You are helpless to deal with that youth. Society is helpless in dealing with the youth. There is no legislation that permits intervention or sanction. That simply is not acceptable when we already have a Young Offenders Act. It specifically provides for youth services, intervention, sanction, probation, curfew, conditions, guidance and psychologists.
The Young Offenders Act provides for that system in each of the provinces. Yet for these young offenders aged 10 and 11, we are not using it. They simply drop outside the system. They do not come within the net. I think Canadians want young offenders of that category dealt with by the Young Offenders Act.
Maybe there is no real family at home. That is often the case for young offenders of this nature. There is no accounting. There is no apology and there is no sanction for these 10 and 11-year-olds.
What kind of message does that send to the young offender of that age? What kind of a message is it? He or she would be totally unsure whether there was any line drawn in the sand, whether there was any sanction, whether or not society was really showing any denunciation for the act.
Sadly yesterday we learned about a case in the United Kingdom. It was not in this country. It is a few thousand miles away. It involved the case of a murder of a
Private Members' Business
2-year-old who was bludgeoned and then left on a railway track. As awful as those details were, I was shocked when I heard that the police were looking for two suspects, youths aged 10 to 12.
If that happened in this country, I say that those youths would by law, if they were caught and if they were of that age group, be simply taken home. They would have to be taken home to their parents. That is it. There is no more sanction. There are no more dealings. A social worker would check into it. That is it. There is no ability to do anything other than to do something to protect the offending child. There is nothing to protect society. That is simply not good enough.
Child welfare legislation is there to protect the young child and not the public. We need legislation that will address protection of the public. Where is the justice now? Where is the sense of proportion? Where is the ability of society to protect itself? Where is the procedure to give those 10 and 11-year-old young offenders access to young offender treatment programs? It just is not there.
On this one item of amending the age category, the Young Offenders Act needs reform. I know members opposite know that. The age must be reduced. I urge members in the House to adopt this reform as one of several which we have to see to. My constituents want these reforms, as do all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate with regard to young offenders.
I have to say right from the very start that I am not in favour of lowering the age from 12 to 10. The minimum age of young offenders prior to the Young Offenders Act being passed in the House in 1984 was certainly discussed not only here in this House but right across the country in each province as well as the two territories.
A lot was taken into consideration. First of all, you have to take a look at the mental capacity of a 10-year-old. While chronologically somebody can be 10, their capacity to understand and comprehend varies greatly. It varies with the individual and the family surroundings in which he or she has been raised.

February 18, 1993
Private Members' Business
Let us just take the capacity of a youngster who is 10 or 11. Does he or she understand the criminal law system? Does he or she understand what it is to go into court and what their legal rights are? I think we would be taking far too much for granted if we ever even gave a thought to lowering the age.
I agree that there are some things within the Young Offenders Act today that need to be amended. I know my colleague mentioned that in his closing remarks. However, it is not lowering the age by any means.
I want to look at a troubled youngster. A 10-year old or an 11-year-old troubled youngster commits a crime. Why? Often it comes down to a family in which there is some sort of dysfunction. Either it is a single parent or, not always, two parents where both of them are working and there is not enough supervision or indeed there is abuse. When I speak of abuse I do not just mean sexual abuse. We get into psychological abuse, emotional abuse, physical abuse. There are all kinds of abuse. Many of our youngster grow up in that today. We need to put more emphasis on the family and ridding ourselves of family violence and family abuse.
Obviously this is a major problem. I understand what my colleague said with regard to two or three cases that he elaborated. One had to do with a youngster in a school who was sexually assaulting. He was 10-years old and sexually assaulting another youngster and then coming back with a pellet gun.
I would have to ask myself, number one, about the principal and counsellors within that school. Certainly some reporting must have been done. Second, when youngsters are apprehended by the police department they are, yes, taken to their house.
They cannot be arrested.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I am not asking that they be arrested but there is something wrong to cause them to commit that particular offence in the beginning. I think it is up to our social services with regard to assisting these youngsters. It may be a family problem and the youngster would have to be removed from the family. That can be done. It can be done through the social services or through the child protection system. It is unfortunate but sometimes it is a lot better for the youngster.
It is clear that the needs of youngsters who are 10 or 11 years old must be looked at and must be reviewed by the
child protection and mental health systems, not by forcing them into family court and not by finding them guilty of a certain criminal crime. Incarceration, you cannot do that to a 10-year-old. Not at all.
What we have to do is strengthen the social services so we could get into the home, into the communities and into building up the family life. That is what is so needed.
Let us talk about the Young Offenders Act. This has been a very volatile subject in my riding and in a lot of ridings right across the country.
First, under the 1984 legislation, it deals with youngsters who are 12 years old through to 17 years old inclusive. I would strongly say that youngsters who are 16 years old and 17 years old should be moved to adult court. They are not young offenders. I would like to see an amendment where we would lower the age from the top down and say that the 12 to 15-year-olds are young offenders. However 16 and 17-year-olds who can have jobs, leave school, drive cars and assume responsibility should be treated like adults.
I feel very strongly there are habitual young offenders and they are the ones who we have to treat more seriously. Any young offender who has been twice convicted of an indictable offence and is back in court for the third time should automatically be moved to adult court.
There are weaknesses in the system. I feel very strongly that there are some amendments that need to be made, but I am not going to say that a youngster of 10 or 11 should fall under the Young Offenders Act. We have to deal with it with our social services, and I know that a lot of those responsibilities are within provincial jurisdiction. I also know that by working with Brighter Futures, which the Minister of National Health and Welfare tabled some months ago, or working with our aboriginal peoples we can certainly improve the system.
However, it is through education, counselling and public awareness that we can improve the situation.
If both parents are working, that is tough. How many members in this House have latchkey kids? How many members in this House are really single parents with full responsibility for their youngster plus a job? There are not very many. It is a big responsibility, so there is a lot more to this than sending youngsters who are 10 years old to jail.
February 18, 1993

Let us look at the young offenders. There are lots of things we can do. We legislate the law, the provinces administer the act along with the courts, and the police department makes all of the decisions about whether to charge or not. We do have problems and a lot are in the court system. The court system is under such stress and strain because of the backlog that there are certain convictions that should not even go into court, such as speeding, unless it is dangerous driving. There are certain tickets that I can pay by sending in a cheque, be it a speeding or parking ticket. We should remove these from the family court system.
What about sentencing charts so that all across our country youngsters in the young offender system who are found guilty and convicted of a similar crime receive a similar sentence? It differs greatly from the city of Calgary to the city of Vancouver.
We can encourage out of city initiations to put the youngsters to work so they understand what an eight-hour day is, be it perhaps in the forestry business or the parks and recreation business, and at the same time teach them a vocation so that they then can carry on in a meaningful way with employment in their future lives. There is education. A lot of these youngsters have dropped out of school. They do not have enough education to get them through society in the coming years.
It is most important that we not only have the young offenders system that we have today but that we set up certain types of work camps for habitual young offenders and teach them a trade.
How about the financial accountability of some of these young offenders? What of those who steal cars for a joy-ride and then damage them? The car is then a write off. Somehow through the insurance system, and even through the income tax system, there could be a charge so that over the period of 10 or 12 years, once they go into the working system, they will slowly have to pay off their financial responsibility to society. That should be put in there.
I absolutely believe that there are many means by which we could strengthen the Young Offenders Act so that youngsters who are 16 and 17 are treated as adults and we get to the habitual young offender, who is 6 per cent of all the young offenders but is doing 80 or 90 per
Private Members' Business
cent of the offences. Those are the people we should be after, not the little kids who are 10 and 11 years old and come from broken families or families who have problems. They need counselling and they need help. I agree.
If there are family problems they should be removed from the family, I agree with my colleague from across the way, but there are certainly ways to help the family without putting these youngsters in jail.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate today. This bill that is before us is proposing to lower the age of people covered by the Young Offenders Act to 10 years from 12 years. Although I sympathize with some of the member's concerns and some of the points made by the member from the government side I do not think, and certainly members of the New Democratic Party would not think, that we should lower the age from 12 years to 10 years.
In this country we spend over $8 billion a year on the justice system right now. Canadians are feeling less safe in this country than they have probably ever felt. The United States has become very serious about building more jails and becoming tougher on offenders but it has a worse record than we do.
The answer is not in making tougher laws and further deterrents. The answer is in other areas. With respect to this bill, yes, there are children who are 10 or 11 or sometimes 7 or 8 years of age who have some severe problems and are a detriment to themselves and the people around them. However, changes should not be made specifically to the Young Offenders Act unless they are linked with increased mental health and social services with the provinces and with federal cost sharing for those services. There must be a broader approach.
A child who is seriously out of control, such as the one mentioned by the hon. member who threatened to use a pellet gun, is a serious problem. A child who is seriously out of control requires long-term, open-ended treatment. That simply cannot be appropriately provided under the definite sentencing framework of the Young Offenders Act. Criminalizing behaviour is not an effective response in dealing with a child with severe behavioural problems.

February 18, 1993
Private Members' Business
The Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General is examining law enforcement and the future of law and order in this country. I want to note the Canadian Police Association position on this issue. It stated before this committee just recently that: "As a society we should also recognize that the solution to crime by younger criminals is not to reduce the age of the Young Offenders Act applicably, but instead to accept the reality that failing to intervene in some cases does the young person and society a greater disservice in the long run. This approach, intervention by provincial authorities in child welfare situations, is obviously fraught with immense difficulties itself. Just because that is so, however, should not deter us from carefully having the courage to make the tough judgments necessary. It will by no means be easy. But to ignore such problems potentially condemns children to a likely worse state".
These are the people who are working on the front lines. These are the police officers who deal with this on a daily basis, and they are taking that approach. Yes, there is a need to deal with this issue. Yes, there is a problem in this area. Yes, there are problems with the Young Offenders Act and they will be looked at.
If we are going to deal with this problem effectively we must have a broader approach. I understand that the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General, which is looking at this area, is going to come out with a recommendation that will say that we must look at preventing crime before it begins by working with the family, and by doing things in this in society that will be preventative in nature. That is the approach this committee is going to take, having looked into it. That is the underlying principle from which we are going to have to deal with this issue and other issues pertaining to law and order.
Although I sympathize with the member's concerns and I agree with him that there is a problem the answer is more in terms of looking at crime prevention and seriously working with the provinces to deal with these incidents. In many cases a deterrent factor is not going to help a child who is 10 or 11. If we do lower the age to 10, what happens when a child who is 8 or 9 commits murder? Are we going to lower the age to 8 then? No.
The way to deal with this issue is to take the broader approach. That is the way we should deal with this issue.
With due respect to the member, I think that would be the better approach.

Mr. Speaker, if the intent of the member who proposed this bill is to express a concern for law and order in Canada I would be standing with him and beside him, because all Canadians want to see a greater level of law and order maintained in our communities. If he wants to specifically recognize that law and order has changed to the point that it is not just adults or young people but children who are now involved in crime then I would also agree with him.
The question is how to handle the situation to obtain more law and order and fewer offences, less criminality. I am not sure that the solution the hon. member is proposing is really an answer, let alone the answer.
We have argued these ages before. I sat on the first Young Offenders Act committee in the seventies when we made the first revision since 1911 or 1921, it was something like that. We had the same problem of making a subjective or arbitrary decision: What would the age of a young offender be? At that time we were dealing with the upper age: Should it be 19, 18, 17, 16, 15 and so forth?
As a matter of fact it was a Conservative member of the committee, Allan Lawrence, the former Attorney General of Ontario, who moved to make the age that we were going to establish 16. The NDP members at the time said it should be 21. I remember making a motion myself saying that we should saw it off at 17, which it is in several of the provinces now.
It was also an issue of jurisdiction. At that point in some provinces it was 16, some 17 and some 18. The question was who would take responsibility for the young offender at that time. Would it be the federal level or the provincial level? If the federal government legislated, that meant the provincial governments had to increase their facilities and their ability for care.
The federal government forcing the provincial governments to increase the numbers of people they had to care for meant that their facilities became overcrowded. As the facilities became overcrowded they put them out onto the street too fast and too soon and there were not enough spaces. All of these kinds of repercussions further undermined law and order.
February 18, 1993

It was a problem of choosing an arbitrary age. In that case, the question was when does a person become an adult? Certainly, all the arguments that were put forward are arguments similar to ones being made now.
It is true that some people become adults at 14 or 15 years old and others never become adults for their entire life. Maybe the age is 25 or maybe it is 30. It is true that this is an arbitrary subjective decision that is not the same for all people in our society.
Similarly the issue of 12, 11, 10, 13, 14, and 15 years of age are all subjective decisions that are different for each person, each child, in each family in each situation. You cannot draw that perfect line.
I think it is generally agreed that the young offender at the other end becomes an adult when they become independent of their parents or away from their parents. We were trying to find that age somewhere in there. Probably in retrospect I think we came up too high. At that time I moved an amendment that it should have been lower and in the same space at the end when a person becomes an adult.
Then at the other end of the range the same thing occurs with a child. I think generally it is perceived that a child becomes a young person probably around the age of puberty because that is when the changes really start to happen. Usually it is around the age of 12.
It is true some people enter puberty at 10 or 11 years or whatever age, but a space has to be picked where most children are. I think to say it is 11 years of age or less is probably too young. As they approach 12 years of age then they come into a new category.
The Young Offenders Act then accommodated the fact that at 12 years of age one can also be a violent criminal. Therefore we allowed in the revisions that a young person at the age of 12 could then be brought before a higher court, to an adult court if necessary and appropriate depending upon the nature of the crime and giving flexibility.
It could be that we could recognize a degree of criminality or allow some sort of a judgmental process which could raise that child to a young offender depending upon maturity and other things. I do not think that is where it is at in the attitudinal sense about how we want
Private Members' Business
to care for children, how we want to care for young offenders and how we want to care for older or adult offenders.
There is the sense that we look at each of them differently. Perhaps for the older offender we are looking at rehabilitation, incarceration for the protection of that person plus society or their victims and the victims of that criminal. Then we are into the field of actual punishment which could go anywhere from emotional punishment to the age-old question of corporal or capital punishment which has been removed from our system. That is another area of debate.
At the adult level we want to apply all of those things. Perhaps in some measure it is to cause correction, in other words to cause correction giving us social behaviour as opposed to anti-social behaviour.
We get down to the bottom end. Let us say the top end is the ultimate criminal who has the least chance of rehabilitation and perhaps none. We always hope that person can be rehabilitated. However, that person is a violent criminal murderer addicted to drugs and alcohol, an almost total reject from our society with very little probability of rehabilitation. Therefore the maximum incarceration would be given for the protection of the public because we cannot bring that person back to the public.
Going to the second level of young offenders surely there is a greater emphasis in the young offender group that there is a possibility for rehabilitation. Therefore rehabilitation needs to be a pre-eminent factor among young offenders.
If we are talking about children we have to have maximum hope for rehabilitation. Surely we are not ready to write off a young person up to the age of 11 or 12 in terms of criminal justice, criminal punishment, retribution and these kinds of things. Hopefully the child is someone we can care for and correct because the patterns have not been so severely established that they cannot be corrected.
We are causing an almost impossible corrections process for a child under the age of 12 because even those systems of care are being totally imperilled. Those systems of care are the first line of care, the home and the family. There is the denuclearization of the family.

February 18, 1993
Adjournment Debate
We are no longer a nuclear family. Our values are different, circumstances are different, and so forth and thus the loss of those family values that normally care and nurture. That is the best place to find it. That is where it works the best, but our system has changed and it does not necessarily exist.
Already we are going to start with problems. Those problems are not identified when a person becomes 12 years old. Ask any grade one teacher and they can tell you which of those kids are already problems and are going to be problems heading toward age 12. However, do they have the resources or the capacity to correct it?
This is an important issue. I do not think the age question is the answer. The answer is in recognizing the symptom of the problem of a child and finding the resources within the community, within our families, to accept that child, love that child, care for that child, rehabilitate him and give him a chance as a young person and an adult in our society.

I will tiy to ignore that demeaning remark from across the aisle simply because that hon. gentleman bears the same characteristics, not nearly so well groomed I might say and not nearly so grey.
I welcome this opportunity to elaborate on a question I put to the hon. Minister of Public Works on September 10 with respect to Old Government House in my riding of Fredericton-York-Sunbury.
Old Government House is a national historic site that represents probably one of the best expressions of the tricultural history of our country, native, English and French, that exists anywhere.
The property is now surplus to the requirements of the Department of Public Works. Over the past four years through the efforts of all three levels of government at the local level we have been preparing a plan and advancing a case for the restoration of that property to be used as the lieutenant governor's office quarters for the province of New Brunswick. It would house the protocol offices of the province of New Brunswick, have a tricultural museum on the second floor and maintenance and historic furniture on the third floor. There would be a very large block of parkland surrounding the property on the banks of the Saint John River for which the city of Fredericton has committed itself to beautification and upkeep.
The general thrust of the proposal is that the Government of Canada would deed the ownership of the land and the property to the province of New Brunswick. The province of New Brunswick would undertake the ownership and the maintenance thereafter.
February 18, 1993

The cost of the restoration is estimated at about $10 million excluding property costs for which the local trilevel steering committee proposed that the federal government consider approximately 70 per cent, the provincial government approximately 30 per cent and the city of Fredericton would put its contribution in in terms of the long-term property maintenance and beautification of the area.
I have suggested in my correspondence with the hon. Minister of Public Works that the federal contribution of approximately $7 million would be divided as follows: $1 million from Public Works Canada itself would be in lieu of ongoing maintenance work. The building is in serious need of repair and there is a major maintenance cost that is presently attributable to it. It will increase as the years go by. Environment Canada under its Canadian Parks Service and National Historic Sites would contribute $1 million. Communications Canada under the Museums Assistance Program and the Cultural Initiatives Program would contribute $2 million. Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency would contribute the final federal equity of $3 million.
The province of New Brunswick as I have said would contribute the remaining $3 million to the capital restoration costs. It would assume in our proposal, and it has not committed to this, the annual maintenance of about $350,000 with the city of Fredericton's ground maintenance being $30,000 per year.
We proposed that this project would be conducted over a five-year period. The initiative is presently with the Minister of Public Works on the federal side and with his counterpart, the Minister of Supply and Services, at the provincial side.
My question for the Minister of Public Works is as to how this matter stands with respect to the proposals I have made to him. Is he ready now to give us a definite and an affirmative answer that will see the opening of this restored Old Government House in Fredericton- York-Sunbury before the turn of the century?

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Public Works I would like to respond to the question by the most hon. member from Fredericton.
Adjournment Debate
He has spent a lot of time not only at home but also in Ottawa working on this project. Not only he and I but the department and the government also agree it is a worth-while project. It is one that is highly desirable. There are not that many buildings in Canada that have the same kind of historic significance. If I understand correctly, that building was actually part of the initial discussions that led up to the Confederation of this great country of ours.
As the member indicated, there has been a trilevel committee of which he was one of the co-chairs. It involved the municipal, provincial and federal levels. It produced a report of the recommendations. Of course, the essence of that report was that they proceed with the renovations to make this a permanent historic site.
As a result of that report, the Department of Public Works has drafted a memorandum. It outlines the work that has to be done as the member has indicated along with an allocation of costs. Under the proposed formula, the federal government would be asked to contribute in land and by other means through the departments that have already been mentioned a total of about 65 per cent of the cost.
Although there has been broad general agreement, there are still some outstanding issues and negotiations are continuing. It is our hope that they will see an early conclusion because we are anxious to move ahead with this project and will give it all our support and encouragement.

Mr. Speaker, on September 15 I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration what he was planning to do to help the unemployed in all of Canada, but especially in the greater Toronto area. At that time 11.7 per cent of the people were jobless. Now, five months later, the situation has not improved very much; it is still over 11 per cent. This means that 212,000 people are looking for work in metro Toronto.
In the same period last year, toward the end of January, beginning of February, 202,000 people were looking for work, which means an increase of 10,000 jobless people in metro Toronto over the past year.

February 18, 1993
Adjournment Debate
The Leader of the Official Opposition announced that job training will be the number one priority when the Liberals form the government. I ask the government of the day why can that government not make people its first priority also?
Toronto used to be the place where people from other parts of Canada came to find jobs. If jobs were not available in the Atlantic region or in the western provinces, people would come and find jobs in Toronto. Now, unemployment is higher in Toronto than in Halifax, Saint John, New Brunswick or Quebec City.
I have constituents in my riding who have never been unemployed for one day in their lives, suddenly at age 55 finding themselves without work and too young to retire. Job retraining is often the only hope for these older workers. These people need help in the new economy, and yet last year the government ran out of money around May or June because of poor planning.
I have many constituents who paid into the UI fund all their lives and when they needed help the government said: Sorry, we goofed, we mismanaged the economy and we cannot help you. Actually, many of them did not even get a sorry; they were very rudely treated when they went to apply for the retraining programs.
My constituents are not looking for handouts. They need a hand up. What assurances can the government give Canadians that the job training fund will not run out of money again? I was pleased that the minister did commit extra funds for the year 1993 of $2.2 billion. Again, are these funds going to run out in May or June, and then for six months people will be coming to their MPs' offices because there are no funds when they go for training?
I did a little research and I found out that the job training fund does not respond to demand. If the money runs out before the end of the fiscal year, Canadians are out of luck, even in the middle of this recession. What kind of economic management is this?
The government has never been capable of managing the economy. The numbers speak for themselves: three million people on welfare; 1.5 million people unemployed. The minister said that the ones who get retraining do go on to better jobs. If that is the case let us put our money where our mouths are. Why should it be just
the employees and the employers paying for retraining. Should not all Canadians pay? When a doctor goes to be trained it is not the medical association and the client that pay. When someone goes to learn to be a teacher, it is not the teaching profession that pays for that education. It comes from general funds. It is the whole country that pays. This should be treated the same way.
Do not put all the training on the backs of the employers and the unemployed. They have been hurt already. I hope the government will have an appropriate answer today.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to review this. When Bill C-21 first went through the House, and was held up in the other house and went back and forth, we did not get much co-operation from the other side. In that bill we introduced training expenditures under the UI program. In 1990, $500 million was committed to training the UI recipients.
Bill C-21 really showed us that this is the way to go and in 1993 we continued our support to training and set up UI training dollars at $2.21 billion. Canada Employment and Immigration over-all expenditures on training and employment assistance is going to reach $3.8 billion in the years 1993-94. With that $3.8 billion, as my colleague has been saying, we are going to provide assistance to over one million Canadians; $300 million of total UI developmental uses goes to address the needs of displaced workers or workers who have a history of long-term attachment to the labour market but who have lost their jobs.
Some 326,000 Canadians are going to receive skills training. Another 162,000 Canadians will train under the Fee Payer Program. We will see $110 million allocated to self-employment assistance and $15 million to assist workers to move to where the jobs are. Over 11,000 Canadians will be assisted under this particular program.
We are also going to see $120 million budgeted for UI job creation in 1993 to assist probably about 31,000 unemployed workers to get back into the work force. Also we will be providing $130 million in work sharing assistance and, therefore, about 160,000 Canadians are going to participate in that particular initiative.
February 18, 1993

I agree with my colleague across the way that training, education and skills training is extremely important. As we see the job market change all around the world, not just here in Canada, but all across Europe, England, Japan, the United States, Central and South America, there is going to be more of a necessity for skills training.
I know that private enterprise, unions and educational institutions are also joining with various governments, not just federal but provincial governments, to realize and emphasize the importance of that. While $3.8 billion may not be enough at this particular time, because of the restraints we are under it is all that we can afford. We have to spend it in the most effective places and get the best bang for our buck.

Mr. Speaker, on February 1 I asked the Prime Minister a question. The question was based on a meeting the Prime Minister had with the premier of Saskatchewan last fall. The Prime Minister had said that if there was a need, the government would be willing to look at some other solutions with respect to agriculture.
I just want to refer to the response. When I rose in the House I asked the Prime Minister exactly what his government was planning to do with respect to agriculture in Saskatchewan as a result of the very poor harvest and the difficulties that exist in Saskatchewan at this time, he responded, and I quote: "This government brought in the GRIP. This government brought in the NISA. Both programs are greatly admired by Saskatchewan farmers".
The GRIP is not greatly admired by Saskatchewan farmers. Saskatchewan farmers do not like the GRIP. They do not like GRIP 91. They do not like GRIP 92. They do not like the Alberta or Manitoba GRIP. They do not like GRIP. That was made abundantly clear at a rally that took place less than a week prior to the day I asked the question. It was made very clear by the 13,000 farmers and others at that rally they did not like the program.
For a government and a party that purports to be such good managers of the economy, I find it strange that the
Adjournment Debate
Prime Minister knows so little about western agriculture, especially considering that his government has spent over $16 billion in direct payments in the last seven or eight years in this field.
Perhaps if the Prime Minister knew more about western agriculture that money would have been spent more wisely.
If the Prime Minister cared more about western agriculture and western Canadians he would not have eliminated one agriculture minister recently and given the other agriculture minister the position of justice minister. The justice ministry is a very full portfolio and that minister will not have time to deal with agriculture. He will be the agriculture minister in name only. We in fact have one agriculture minister.
It seems clear that the government has abandoned this area, that it has lost interest in this area, and we in western Canada are going to suffer for it.
We do not want to hear a litany of all the things the government has done, because they have not worked. Farmers and rural people, in fact all western Canadians, want to know what approach this government is going to take toward agriculture in the future.
We know there has to be consultation with the provinces. We know there have to be new programs developed. It is going to take the leadership of this government to initiate those programs.
What plan does the government have with respect to the future of agriculture? Oftentimes when governments do not have an answer they simply stand on their laurels and brag about all the things they have done.
I hope the government will not do that this time. Please tell western Canadians, please tell the people watching the parliamentary channel right now or those who will be reading Hansard what this government is planning to do with agriculture. What is the future direction with respect to agriculture in this country?

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal government has supported farmers at an unprecedented level. We are going to continue to do so. We are going to continue to use all the safety nets which happen to include NISA and GRIP.

February 18, 1993
Adjournment Debate
Those programs were developed by the producers through consultation with the agriculture minister and indeed the Governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. There was three-way participation. This was not by any means a unilateral agreement.
From 1985 to 1992 the federal government has provided close to $17 billion in direct payments to agriculture. Out of that $6.6 billion has gone to Saskatchewan. Much of this support was provided to overcome problems of drought and the effects of the international grain export subsidy war.
This year payments under crop insurance in GRIP alone are expected to increase to between $800 million and $1.1 billion in Saskatchewan, to which we are going to be adding $170 million from the agreement worked out a few weeks ago. I think my colleague mentioned the agreement that was worked out with that particular province.
In addition, we still have an offer of $63 million with Saskatchewan if we can cost share with the province. That represents a significant amount of money for a single province at a time when all of us at all levels are under restraint and other programs are being cut.
This government recognizes there are problems. We know that. We are making our programs as responsive as possible. The problems cannot be solved by more federal payments. The industry also needs long-term solutions and we would all like to see better prices. We want to see improved market opportunities, diversification and rural development opportunities. These are areas that we continue to work through.
We will be able to put more emphasis on GATT with regard to removing the subsidy war between the U.S. and the EC. Western diversification kicks in there as well.
I think the member will find that we have done a great deal.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 18, 1992 I put a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I asked the minister if he would establish a full and independent inquiry, independent of governments, bureaucrats and
politicians, with regard to a very serious issue concerning tainted blood.
Early in the 1980s the blood supply in many countries, including Canada, was contaminated by HIV. A study conducted by the Canadian Haemophilia Society provides reasonable grounds, and I underline the words reasonable grounds, to suspect that hundreds of blood transfused persons within Canada have yet to be notified of their HIV positive status.
The minister of health unfortunately rejected my call for an independent inquiry based on the grounds that it was not needed. He did however, to be fair and objective, say that he would consider an inquiry if it were needed to maintain Canada's faith in the country's blood management system and if the Red Cross and the Canadian Haemophilia Society were to request an inquiry.
On December 3, 1992 the Canadian Haemophilia Society called for a full independent investigation into the current blood system. Also five out of the six witnesses who have appeared before the subcommittee on health and welfare have called for a full independent inquiry.
I would hope that the parliamentary secretary, a very able and a very knowledgeable individual on the particular subject matter at hand, would avail of the minister as well as the department to concede to the request for an independent inquiry. To underline the sincerity of the request, I wish to tell the Chair and hon. members that the kind of inquiry we seek will certainly go back into years in which members of the opposition were in fact members of the government. This is not a witch-hunt of any sort. This is an opportunity to clear the air, to have an independent inquiry, in order to put some of these major issues to rest.
I would hope the parliamentary secretary responsible would respond in the affirmative, whereby careful and prudent consideration would once again be given to this request in view of the evidence which has come forward from reliable, sincere and responsible individuals following the issue for quite some time.
I hope the parliamentary secretary, in her usual way, could give me the kind of answer that would give
February 18, 1993

assurances to those people who are in desperate need at this time.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the contamination of the blood supply in the 1980s by the HIV virus really represented a source of great personal tragedy for many people around the world. Indeed Canada did not escape.
According to the federal government's extraordinary assistance plan for HIV infected blood and blood product recipients, 928 Canadians were infected with HIV in this manner between 1978 and the implementation of the blood screening in 1985.
Others of course have been infected from transfusions that were received between 1985 and the establishment of the assistance plan in 1989. To the best of anyone's knowledge, these cases are associated with donors who through a brief window period before having developed any detectable sign of HIV infection donated blood.
While anything less than perfect is really very lamentable, today we do have a high standard of security and quality control in the blood system. However I would like to review the role of the federal government. We are a regulator. Under the Food and Drugs Act, Health and Welfare Canada has been responsible for the regulation of manufactured blood products like factor 8 and factor 9 for the treatment of coagulation disorders like haemophilia since the inception of these particular products.
The first factor 8 was licensed for sale in Canada in 1969. Also under this authority in November 1984 the department required all manufacturers of factor 8 and factor 9 to heat treat all products for use in Canada by a method known to inactivate HIV.
The second component of the department's role is as national health advisor to Canadians. Through the department we report the results of surveillance of AIDS and we started as early as 1982. We have provided regular comprehensive information on AIDS since then.
The third element is the department's role in the blood supply was as a non-voting advisory member of the Canadian Blood Committee. The federal government relinquished its non-voting advisory role in overseeing the blood supply in 1989 when the provincial and territorial ministers of health agreed to establish the Canadian Blood Agency.
As my colleague mentioned the subcommittee of the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare is studying this particular issue of HIV transmitted disease in the blood supply during a specific period, looking mainly at prior to 1985.
Adjournment Debate
I know there are numerous witnesses we have not heard from yet but I can say that under the direction of our chairman from Delta in B.C., who is a physician, the committee will be bringing forth recommendations.
I am a member on that committee and look forward to hearing as many people as possible. We hope to come forward with recommendations that will be satisfactory to all members in the House.

Mr. Speaker, on February 12 I put a question to the minister of employment and asked him why he was proposing to totally deny unemployment insurance benefits to those who quit their jobs but could not prove just cause, when in 1990 his government brought in a penalty of seven to 12 weeks for the same matter.
I asked him why this excessive new penalty. Was the penalty he imposed in 1990 of up to 12 weeks not harsh and tough enough? If it was not, where were the studies to show it was not? Where were the evaluation studies? Where were the assessment studies?
Why after two years with a new rather harsh penalty of seven to 12 weeks was it necessary to bring in this new total disqualification of these individuals, especially when very often the matter of just cause is not clear cut? It is very difficult to prove and takes a long time to prove. It takes from two to three months on average to prove. We had one case in Montreal where it took up to two years.
Why is it necessary to have this absolute total disallowance of unemployment insurance benefits when you have another rule in the Unemployment Insurance Act that says you can only continue to receive benefits as long as you are ready and available for work?
I am saying this new proposed penalty is disproportionate to the offence. Under the present law a real abuser, the person who wants to quit without just cause and simply take a holiday, can be subject to a 12-week penalty. He then becomes eligible for benefits but if he is not ready and available for work he is totally disqualified. He does not get any unemployment insurance.
On the other hand is the person who wants to work but quits a job and has a just cause but cannot prove it because it is difficult to prove. Under the present law that person would get the 12-week penalty but would then qualify and immediately start looking for work. He would get unemployment insurance because he would be ready and available for work. He would be out searching for a new job.

February 18, 1993
Adjournment Debate
Under this proposed law that same person would have no chance for any benefits whatsoever. He leaves his job. He believes he has just cause but cannot prove it. He gets turned down for one reason or other and is totally disqualified even though he is looking for a new job.
He does not want to sit at home; he does not want to go to Florida; he wants to work. He could not stand the situation he was in for one reason or another. Even under the new rules that were proposed yesterday under Bill C-113, he just may not be able to get his evidence together because it may be a grey area or an unclear area but he wants to work.
I want the minister to show me the evidence that this new penalty of seven to 12 weeks imposed in 1990 in Bill C-21 was not tough enough. Why did we have to go to this total disqualification, especially when we will have another provision in the law that says that if you are not ready and available for work at all times you totally lose your benefits anyway? I support that provision in the law.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond today. The member is correct. In 1990 I served on a committee where we spent a lot of time trying to deal with that bill. It covered a number of improvements, a number of reforms, one of which attempted to get a better balance between the training and retraining of workers, rather than strictly the insurance aspect, and staying out of work and collecting UI with no preparation whatsoever for returning to the work force.
Obviously with the restraint the government is faced with, there is no question that UI is a very big factor in
the country's economy. It is over $20 billion a year. The current deficit in the UI fund is in excess of $4 billion.
There are a number of people who are using the UI fund who have quit without just cause. This government does not feel that the average worker in this country should be forced through their premiums to support people who leave their jobs for no just cause.
It is an opportunity in trying to address the restraints that are required to re-establish unemployment insurance with the insurance basis, to insure those who through no fault of their own have left their jobs and this government does not feel that the other workers should be forced to support them.
There have been a number of changes brought about in the new release of the bill. We have heard from not only members opposite but from people across the country. There is concern about how this is going to be applied. There will have to be extreme care taken by the government. It has added eight other major reasons of just cause. They were there before but they are there to try to ensure that the people across the country who have a legitimate concern will realize that this is not meant to penalize them and that the insurance program will work well for the unemployed people across Canada.
